deep.reconstruction:
The page has two parts: a table of wire data, and resistances computed from it.

PART 1 – WIRE TABLE ('Drahte'). For each wire gauge number (Nro 2, 4, …, 18) Gauss records:
- λ = length in mm of wire that weighs 1 gram ('1 gr = λ mm'). This is the reciprocal of the linear density: mass per mm = 1/λ g.
- ρ = diameter ('Dicke') in mm.
- the product λρ².

Why λρ² (my explanation): for a homogeneous cylinder of density δ (g/mm³), 1 g = δ·(π/4)ρ²·λ. Hence λρ² = 4/(πδ), which should be the same for every gauge of the same metal. The column is therefore a consistency and density check on the measured diameters.

The values run 137.07, 136.89, 136.08, 126.15, 139.35, 121.17, (Nro 14 blank), 106.21, 106.18.
- The thick wires (Nro 2–6) give about 136–137, i.e. δ = 4/(π·137) ≈ 0.0093 g/mm³ = 9.3 g/cm³. That is roughly copper, about 4% high.
- The thin wires (Nro 16, 18) give about 106, i.e. ≈ 12 g/cm³. This is physically implausible for copper. It shows that the small diameters were measured too small (or the wire is a different material).
- So the column documents the unreliability of the diameter measurements of the fine wires.

The products do not reproduce exactly from the 3-decimal ρ printed (e.g. 95.4·1.198² = 136.92, not 137.07). Inverting Gauss's products gives ρ = 1.1987, 0.8929, 0.6768, 0.5170, 0.3501, 0.2491, 0.1202, 0.1025. So Gauss evidently computed λρ² from more precise diameters and wrote ρ rounded or truncated to 3 decimals.

A 'Tragvermögen' (load-bearing/breaking load) column gives 2300 g for Nro 16 and 700 g for Nro 18.

PART 2 – RESISTANCES. The unit is the resistance of a wire 1 m long weighing 1 g. Resistance is proportional to L/A, and A is proportional to (mass per unit length) = 1000/λ g per m for L in metres. So in this unit, R = L·λ/1000 = L²/m, with m the mass in grams. (This is mass-resistivity bookkeeping; it assumes all wires are the same metal.) The worked cases:
- Nro 10, 66.5 m: R = 66.5·1.1367 = 75.59 ✓.
- Nro 16, 60 m: R = 60·7.3533 = 441.20 ✓.
- Inductor (+5 m), Nro 12, 224 m: R = 224·1.953 = 437.47 ≈ 437.5 ✓.
- Multiplicator, Nro 12, 248 m: Gauss writes 479.3, but 248·1.953 = 484.3. 479.3 corresponds to 245.4 m. The line contains cancelled figures, so the length was perhaps changed.

Finally: 'Electromotorische Kraft von 1074 Windungen bei unserm Multiplicator, Doppelstoss über beide grosse Stäbe' = 444860. This is the induced EMF for a double induction impulse with both large bar magnets, presumably in Gauss–Weber absolute (magnetic) units. Its derivation is not on this page and it cannot be checked here. The next page records winding counts on coils (98, 159, 1050), consistent with this induction-apparatus context. The previous page is dated 12 May 1842.
errors: Multiplicator line: 248 m of Nro 12 (λ = 1953.0 mm/g) gives 484.3 in Gauss's unit, not 479.3. 479.3 corresponds to about 245.4 m. Either a slip or an uncorrected length (the line has cancelled entries).

The λρ² values are not reproducible from the rounded ρ as written (e.g. Nro 2: 136.92 vs 137.07; Nro 18: 105.25 vs 106.18). Most likely they were computed from unrounded diameters, so this is not an arithmetic error.

λρ² is far from constant (106 to 139). The implied density of about 12 g/cm³ for Nro 16/18 is physically impossible for copper, so the fine-wire diameters are measured too small. Gauss leaves this inconsistency uncommented.
Tragvermögen 2300 g vs 700 g for diameters 0.120 vs 0.102 mm (area ratio about 1.4) is a strength ratio of about 3.3. This is odd and suggests a different wire quality or a misplaced entry.

results.what: Consistency check of wire diameter vs length per gram via λρ² = 4/(πδ)
results.modern_name: Linear density / gauge-density relation for cylindrical wire

results.what: Relative resistance unit: wire 1 m long weighing 1 g; R = L·λ/1000 = L²/m
results.modern_name: Mass resistivity (resistance proportional to L²/mass for a given material)
results.usually_credited_to: standard 19th-century practice (cf. Matthiessen's mass-resistivity work, 1860s); relative resistance units of the era, e.g. Jacobi's etalon (1848)

results.what: Numerical EMF of a double induction impulse for a 1074-turn multiplier (444860)
results.modern_name: Induced EMF in absolute (magnetic) units, Gauss–Weber induction experiments
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss and Weber (Göttingen magnetic/induction work, 1830s–40s); Weber's absolute EMF/resistance units (1851)

deep.surprise_reason: Laboratory bookkeeping on wire gauges and relative resistances in a mass-based unit, part of the well-known Gauss–Weber induction work. Nothing beyond routine experimental physics of the period.

transcription_corrections: '66m5' should be read as 66.5 m (confirmed by 66.5 × 1.1367 = 75.59).
Nro 16 product: the overwritten entry reads 106.21 (an earlier 105.x is struck). 106.21 is consistent with ρ ≈ 0.1202.
Header: the struck-out unit next to '1 gr =' is 'mm'. λ is the length in mm per gram, not '1 gr = mm' as a heading equation.
